headline: Fiona the hippo died. It started with a knit hat.
summary: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo hippo born six weeks early in 2017, died Thursday. Eleven days ago a visitor tossed a knit hat in the air, a ceiling fan caught it and flung it into her pool, and she swallowed it. Vets gave her treats, tried a vibration plate from a horse farm and scoped her with a 9-foot camera. Surgery on a grown hippo isn't an option.
cover_answer: Hippo skin is two inches thick, and they can't be kept dry.
table_question: An accident nobody could have planned. Is anyone to blame?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Fiona the hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo died on Thursday. A hat fell into her pool and she swallowed it, and it got stuck inside her, the way a sock jams a vacuum cleaner. Her doctors tried for eleven days to help it come out. They couldn't. A lot of people loved Fiona, and it's okay to be sad.
5-7.why: A stuck hat they can picture. The sadness is allowed, and named.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole thing, so the script gives them the hat, stuck the way a sock jams a vacuum. Cantor's work says this age reads a parent's face before the words, so say she died plainly and let the sadness sit. Expect 'can they get a new Fiona?' No. There are other hippos at the zoo, and they are not her.

8-12.script: A visitor at the Cincinnati Zoo tossed a knit hat in the air. A ceiling fan flung it into Fiona's pool, and she swallowed it. A hippo's stomach has several chambers, like a cow's, so the hat hid. Vets can't operate on a grown hippo. An accident, then a stuck hat, then a body that couldn't clear it.
8-12.why: An accident, a stuck hat, a body that can't clear it. No villain.
8-12.why_long: At ten a child wants the chain of cause and effect and wants to know whose fault it was. The script runs it: a tossed hat, a fan, a stomach with chambers that hid it, a body too big to operate on. The mechanism matters more than blame. Expect 'why don't they ban hats?' Zoos ask you to keep things out of the habitats. That is the rule here.

13-17.script: Why couldn't they just operate? Hippo skin is two inches thick, they're hard to anesthetize, and she'd need days out of water to heal. So the vets bet on her passing it herself. Right call, or too long a wait? Second: the zoo calls it a freak accident. Does that settle who's responsible?
13-17.why: Two things to hold: the vets tried everything, and she still died.
13-17.why_long: At thirteen they can hold two true things: the vets did everything the articles describe, and Fiona still died. Kuhn says argument is a practised skill, so the script asks whether waiting was the right call rather than telling them. Expect 'would surgery have saved her?' Nobody knows. The specialists said it wasn't an option for a grown hippo.

5-7.a: She wasn't in pain at first, and her doctors stayed with her the whole time. They gave her treats and even let her sniff coffee, which she liked.

8-12.q: Why didn't they just cut it out?
8-12.a: Her skin is two inches thick, and she'd need days out of water to heal.
No one's, the zoo says. A fan flung the hat through a gap.

13-17.a: Skin two inches thick, and days out of water to heal. Vets said no.

13-17.q: Did the zoo wait too long?
13-17.a: They say they tried everything. Nobody in the articles says otherwise.
